screens.title: Building and Deployment Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Bringing a game to players means more than finishing levels and scripts. In this lesson you will learn the practical steps to turn your Unity project into an app or executable for Windows, WebGL, Android and other targets. We will use Unity's Build Settings and Player Settings as the control center: select target platforms, add scenes, and set identity and presentation options like company name, product name, icons, and splash screens. You'll also learn about platform requirements such as the Android SDK, NDK and JDK, and how different targets produce different output files — a Windows executable and data folder, a WebGL folder of H T M L and JavaScript, or a signed Android APK. Finally, we'll introduce runtime content strategies: Asset Bundles and Addressables, which let you deliver large or updated content without rebuilding the whole game. By the end you should understand how to configure builds, what can fail, and where to test. Think about a target platform you care about — what is the smallest change that would let you run your game there?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Building & Deployment
Building and Deployment Strategies
From editor to executable: use Build Settings and Player Settings to target platforms reliably.

In this module you'll practice: choosing the right platform, adding scenes to a build, and configuring identity and presentation so your game installs and runs correctly. We'll highlight common platform traps such as missing bundle identifiers and unsigned APKs.

You'll also get an introduction to runtime content strategies—Asset Bundles and Addressables—to keep downloads small and update content without shipping a full patch.

Explore Key Topics
Build Settings
Choose platform, add scenes, and start the build pipeline.
Player Settings
Set company, product, icons, splash and platform IDs.
Asset Delivery
Use Addressables for dynamic loading and updates.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Visual: Build pipeline overview
Cards show: selected platform, scenes list, and output folder. This helps you map editor choices to resulting files.
Platform: WebGL
Scenes: MainScene
Why this matters
A correct build pipeline avoids store rejections and runtime surprises. Plan identity, signing, and testing early.
Key Takeaway

Treat Build Settings and Player Settings as product-level configuration: they determine how your game appears, what platforms it runs on, and what files you ship.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this section you will be able to prepare and execute platform builds, configure player identity and presentation, and plan distribution steps for desktop, web, and mobile. First, you'll learn to configure Unity's Build Settings to select target platforms and include the correct scenes. That matters because missing scenes or wrong targets are one of the most common build-time mistakes. Second, you'll learn how to customize Player Settings for company name, product name, icons and splash screens so your app presents correctly to users and stores. Third, you'll run the build process to create executables or app bundles and inspect the produced files. Finally, you'll begin to plan post-build steps like signing APKs, hosting WebGL files, and testing on devices. Each skill reduces friction when you deliver to players. For example, setting a correct Bundle Identifier prevents store upload errors; testing the build on hardware reveals performance differences the editor won't show. Keep these goals handy as we move into the practical steps.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Practice
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide explains how you will prove competency. For configuring Build Settings, you'll show you can pick a platform and add scenes so the built game contains the intended content. A concrete example: add MainScene and build a Windows executable that runs the rotating cube scene. For Player Settings, you'll set Company Name and Product Name so the OS and task manager show the expected labels, and assign a default icon so your executable has a custom icon. For executing builds, you'll create Build folders for Windows and WebGL, run the builds, and verify the output files open or can be hosted locally. Finally, for content delivery, you'll describe where Addressables would fit — mark assets as Addressable and explain how remote hosting lets you update content without a full rebuild. Common misconceptions to avoid: treating Editor play as equivalent to a real build, or skipping keystore configuration for mobile. Each objective ends with a short practical milestone you can demonstrate or explain.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Learning Objectives — Applied
How you'll prove each objective
Short, practical deliverables you can perform in the editor.
Build Settings

Mnemonic

Common Mistake

screens.title: Unity Build Settings — the central hub
screens.narratorSegment: Unity's Build Settings window is the central hub that turns your project into a platform-specific package. A build includes scenes, compiled C# scripts, processed assets, and platform libraries. To create a build you first select a target platform — for example, Windows Standalone, WebGL, Android or iOS — then add the scenes you want included. Adding a scene to the Build Settings ensures its content is packaged in the final build. Different platforms cause Unity to re-import or re-compile assets with target-specific options, so switching platforms may take time. A concrete example: selecting WebGL and adding MainScene produces an H T M L/JavaScript/data folder suitable for hosting on a web server. A common misconception is to rely solely on editor play: editor behavior can mask platform differences such as file input and output or graphics support. Another important point: some platforms require external tooling; building Android needs a configured Android SDK, NDK and a JDK in Unity Preferences. If those are missing, builds will fail or warn. Takeaway: treat Build Settings as an explicit checklist — pick the platform, verify scenes, and confirm any required SDKs before pressing Build. How might you verify the correct scenes are included without running the full game?

keyIdea.title: Build Settings essence
keyIdea.text: Choose target platform and included scenes carefully — that selection determines what Unity packages and how assets are imported for the build.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Build Settings
Definition
A control panel where you select the target platform and scenes to include in the exported build.
Platform selection
Switching platform can re-import assets and change build outputs.
Scenes in Build
Only scenes added here are packaged into the final build.
Required tools
Android builds need SDK, NDK and JDK set in Preferences; missing tools block or break builds.
Key Takeaway

Confirm target platform and scenes before building. Missing a scene is a common and avoidable error.

Practical check: Validate a build setup
Use this quick checklist before pressing Build or Build And Run.
Checklist
  • • Target platform selected and switched.
  • • Required scenes added to the list.
  • • Player Settings identity and presentation configured.
  • • Platform-specific SDKs configured (if required).
Concrete example
Select WebGL, add MainScene, set memory size in WebGL settings, then click Build to create a WebGL folder for hosting.
Common misconception
Don't assume Editor Play equals final build. Platform differences in file APIs, performance and available runtime features can change behavior.
Try this
Switch to Android, then back to Windows and observe asset re-import messages — this signals platform-specific processing.

screens.title: Player Settings — identity and presentation
screens.narratorSegment: Player Settings control how your game identifies itself to the operating system and to players. Core fields include Company Name and Product Name; these values affect the executable title, task manager entries, and store listing metadata. You also set Version, Default Icon and the Splash Image here. For standalone builds you control Resolution and Presentation — default screen size, fullscreen mode, and whether the player window is resizable. Platform-specific sections expose important options: Android shows Bundle Identifier, Minimum and Target A P I Levels, Scripting Backend choices like Mono or IL2CPP, architectures such as ARMv7 or ARM64, and Keystore configuration for signing APKs. WebGL has Compression Format, Memory Size and Template options. A concrete example: in the hands-on we set Company Name to "Cohortia" and Product Name to "MyAwesomeGame" so the produced executable shows that identity. A common mistake is forgetting the Bundle Identifier or keystore for mobile uploads; this blocks publishing. Takeaway: set identity values early and keep platform-specific settings in your release checklist so builds and store submissions are consistent. Player Settings — identity and presentation means player settings determine user-facing identity and many platform-specific build requirements; set them deliberately to avoid store and runtime issues.. In practical terms, company name, product name, icons, splash, and per-platform options. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Player Settings
Core fields explained
These values affect how your game appears to users and to distribution platforms.
Company & Product Name
Controls the executable title and store metadata. Example: Company "Cohortia", Product "MyAwesomeGame".
Icon & Splash
Assign a Default Icon and configure the splash. Note: extensive splash customization requires Unity Pro.
Resolution & Presentation
Set default resolution, fullscreen mode and window resize behavior for standalone builds.
Other Settings (per-platform)
Platform tabs expose bundle identifiers, scripting backend, architectures and signing options.
Common Mistake

Leaving bundle identifiers or keystore unset for mobile; this prevents store uploads or signed packages.

Platform examples
Quick reference of per-platform settings to check before building.
Android
Bundle Identifier, Minimum API Level, Target API, Scripting Backend (Mono/IL2CPP), ARMv7/ARM64, Keystore signing.
WebGL
Compression Format (e.g. Brotli), Memory Size, Template options for hosting.
Quick action
Set Company/Product early and keep versioning consistent to prevent store confusion and rebuild pain.
Key Takeaway

Set identity and signing details early. Missing per-platform settings are the fastest way to block deployment.

screens.title: Platform specifics: Android vs WebGL
screens.narratorSegment: Different platforms require different tooling, outputs and testing strategies. Android builds require platform toolchains: the Android SDK, NDK and a Java Development Kit must be installed and configured in Unity's Preferences. You also need to set a Bundle Identifier (a unique string such as com. YourCompany. YourGame), pick minimum and target A P I levels, choose a scripting backend (Mono for faster iteration, IL2CPP for performance and compatibility), select supported architectures and configure a Keystore to sign your APK. Omission of any of these steps will usually stop a successful publish. WebGL builds produce H T M L, JavaScript, and data files that must be hosted on a web server; you typically set compression (Brotli recommended) and memory size in WebGL Player Settings. A practical example: after building WebGL you can host the output with a simple local server and open the game in a browser. A common misconception is expecting mobile debug builds to behave identically to release-signed builds; signing and A P I levels affect runtime and store acceptance. Closing question: what platform-specific checklist will you run before your next build?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Android vs WebGL
Android — tooling & signing
Requires SDK, NDK and JDK configured. Set Bundle Identifier, API levels, scripting backend and Keystore.
  • • Bundle Identifier: unique app ID (e.g., com.YourCompany.YourGame).
  • • Scripting Backend: Mono for iteration, IL2CPP for performance/compatibility.
  • • Keystore: required to sign APKs for store upload.
Common pitfall: missing keystore or incorrect bundle id blocks publishing.
WebGL — outputs & hosting
Produces HTML, JavaScript and data files that must be hosted. Configure Compression and Memory Size for runtime behavior.
  • • Compression Format: Brotli recommended for best compression.
  • • Memory Size: set appropriate memory for complex games.
  • • Template: choose WebGL template that suits your hosting setup.
Test tip: host locally with a simple server to observe Debug.Log messages in the browser console.
Quick local hosting example
After building WebGL, open a terminal in the Build/WebGL folder and run the simple Python server to host files for testing.
python -m http.server 8000
Then open http://localhost:8000 to test the built WebGL content and view logs in the browser developer console.

screens.title: Platform-specific code with preprocessor directives
screens.narratorSegment: Sometimes you need platform-specific behavior in C#. Unity's preprocessor directives let you include or exclude code at compile time depending on the selected build target. This is a compile-time decision, not a runtime check, so the excluded code isn't present in the final build for that target. A concrete example is logging different messages or using AndroidJavaObject on Android and browser calls on WebGL. The provided sample uses directives like hash-if UNITY_STANDALONE_WIN, UNITY_ANDROID and UNITY_WEBGL to conditionally compile blocks. A common misconception is to think these directives evaluate at runtime; they do not. If you need runtime branching within a single binary, use Application. platform checks instead. Use preprocessor directives to avoid compilation errors for platform-specific APIs and to keep unwanted code out of a build. Try this: add the example script to a GameObject, build for Windows and then for WebGL; observe which messages appear, and note that platform-only APIs are not included in incompatible builds. What platform-specific APIs does your project require? Platform-specific code with preprocessor directives means use preprocessor directives to include platform-specific code at compile time and avoid cross-platform compilation issues.. In practical terms, write code that compiles only for certain build targets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Preprocessor purpose
keyIdea.text: Use preprocessor directives to include platform-specific code at compile time and avoid cross-platform compilation issues.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Preprocessor Directives
Concept
Directives like #if UNITY_ANDROID control which code is compiled for each platform.

Use preprocessor directives when you need to reference APIs available only on certain platforms. This prevents compile errors and keeps platform-specific logic out of incompatible builds.

Misconception
These directives are not runtime checks. Code excluded by a directive is never present in the final build for that platform.
Example C# (place on a MonoBehaviour)
// Example of platform-specific code using preprocessor directives
using UnityEngine;

public class PlatformSpecificFeature : MonoBehaviour
{
    void Start()
    {
#if UNITY_STANDALONE_WIN
        Debug.Log("Running on Windows PC!");
        // Windows-specific code
#elif UNITY_ANDROID
        Debug.Log("Running on Android device!");
        // Android-specific code, e.g., using AndroidJavaObject
        Handheld.Vibrate(); // Example for Android
#elif UNITY_WEBGL
        Debug.Log("Running in WebGL browser!");
        // WebGL-specific code, e.g., JavaScript interaction
#else
        Debug.Log("Running on an unknown platform.");
#endif
    }
}
Note: preprocessor symbols are provided by Unity based on your selected build target.
Key Takeaway

Use compile-time directives to isolate platform-only code; use runtime checks only when a single binary must support multiple platforms simultaneously.

screens.title: Running the Build and Understanding Output
screens.narratorSegment: When you press Build in Unity, the editor moves through a sequence: it compiles your C# scripts, processes and converts assets for the chosen platform, resolves dependencies, and then packages everything into platform-specific files. The result is not a single monolithic file in most cases. For a Windows standalone build you get an executable and a companion data folder; for WebGL you get H T M L, JavaScript, and data files; for Android you typically get an APK or an AAB. Understanding the contents of the build folder helps you diagnose missing assets, platform crashes, and distribution steps. For example, missing scenes show up as empty runtime behavior because those scenes were not included in Build Settings. Large textures or unused assets can bloat the data files and slow build and download times. A practical way to inspect the output is to open the Build folder and confirm the executable or primary host file alongside the data and library files. If you see a small executable and a large data file, the data file is where your assets live. During long builds, Unity writes a log; checking the Editor log for warnings and errors after a build often points to missing references, shader compilation issues, or platform-specific conversion problems. Keep a habit of testing the built output on target hardware and reading build logs to catch asset or script problems that do not appear in the editor. What in your build output would you check first when a game fails to start?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter: Building & Deployment › Build Execution

Running the Build and Understanding Output

What Unity produces and how to inspect the generated files for troubleshooting.

Eyebrow: Build Execution
Process Summary
  • Compile C# scripts into assemblies and IL2CPP where configured.
  • Convert textures, audio, and shaders for the target platform.
  • Package executable or host files plus data, libraries, and streaming assets.
  • Write Editor log and detailed build warnings that help debugging.
Quick Checklist
Confirm all required scenes are added to Build Settings.
Check Editor log for missing references or shader errors after a failed build.
Key Takeaway

Inspect the build folder and Editor log first; they tell you what Unity packaged and what went wrong.

Build Output Example
Platform: Windows Standalone
Builds/Windows/
  MyAwesomeGame.exe
  MyAwesomeGame_Data/
    resources.assets
    managed/
      Assembly-CSharp.dll
    globalgamemanagers
    sharedassets0.assets
  UnityPlayer.dll
The executable is small; most game content sits in the _Data folder. That data contains assets, managed code, and native libraries.
Common Build Warnings
  • Missing references to prefabs or scenes.
  • Shader compilation failures for the target GPU.
  • Large textures not marked for compression—inflates data size.
What to Inspect
  • Editor log: step-by-step build messages and file paths.
  • Size of data files to find unexpectedly large assets.
  • Platform-specific library errors in the console or logs.

screens.title: Packaging for Platforms: APK, IPA, EXE, and Web Builds
screens.narratorSegment: Different target platforms require different packaging and signing procedures. For Windows and Mac you typically distribute the executable plus its data folder as a zip or installer. For Android you produce an APK or Android App Bundle; that package must be signed with a keystore before uploading to Google Play. The keystore is a security artifact that verifies you as the publisher and prevents tampering; Unity references a keystore in Player Settings when building for Android. For iOS you generate an Xcode project and then create an IPA using Apple’s signing system and certificates. WebGL produces H T M L, JavaScript, and data files that you host on a web server; because browsers enforce different resource loading rules, you will typically serve WebGL builds from an HTTP server and set appropriate compression or caching on the server. Preparing for distribution means you must decide how you will package the build (zip, installer, store upload), configure versioning consistently, and ensure identifiers and signing are correct. A common mistake is forgetting to set the Bundle Identifier or keystore, which blocks store uploads. Another is shipping development keys or leaving debug logging enabled, which can expose internals. Before uploading a mobile build, verify version numbers and test installing the signed APK on devices. For WebGL, run a local server to test because simply opening the H T M L file in a browser may fail due to security restrictions. Successful distribution depends on proper signing, unique identifiers, and testing on the actual delivery path.

narration.text: Different target platforms require different packaging and signing procedures. For Windows and Mac you typically distribute the executable plus its data folder as a zip or installer. For Android you produce an APK or Android App Bundle; that package must be signed with a keystore before uploading to Google Play. The keystore is a security artifact that verifies you as the publisher and prevents tampering; Unity references a keystore in Player Settings when building for Android. For iOS you generate an Xcode project and then create an IPA using Apple’s signing system and certificates. WebGL produces H T M L, JavaScript, and data files that you host on a web server; because browsers enforce different resource loading rules, you will typically serve WebGL builds from an HTTP server and set appropriate compression or caching on the server. Preparing for distribution means you must decide how you will package the build (zip, installer, store upload), configure versioning consistently, and ensure identifiers and signing are correct. A common mistake is forgetting to set the Bundle Identifier or keystore, which blocks store uploads. Another is shipping development keys or leaving debug logging enabled, which can expose internals. Before uploading a mobile build, verify version numbers and test installing the signed APK on devices. For WebGL, run a local server to test because simply opening the H T M L file in a browser may fail due to security restrictions. Successful distribution depends on proper signing, unique identifiers, and testing on the actual delivery path.

keyIdea.text: Packaging and signing vary by platform; keystores and bundle identifiers are essential for mobile store distribution, and WebGL needs hosting.

content.html:
Module 6 › Packaging & Distribution

Packaging for Platforms: APK, IPA, EXE, and Web Builds

Understand how each platform expects your build and what extra steps are required for store delivery.

Eyebrow: Packaging & Distribution
Platform Packaging Overview
Windows / Mac
Executable + Data folder. Distribute as a ZIP or installer.
Android
APK / AAB. Requires keystore signing and a unique bundle identifier.
iOS
Export Xcode project and sign with Apple certificates to produce an IPA.
WebGL
HTML, JS, and data files. Host on an HTTP server and enable compression/caching.
Keystore & Bundle Identifier
  • Keystore: Android signing file that proves developer identity. Set this in Player Settings before building a release APK.
  • Bundle Identifier: Unique reverse-DNS string (for example, com.cohortia.myawesomegame) needed for mobile store submission.
  • Keep keystore files secure and back them up; losing a keystore prevents updating a published app with the same identity.
Distribution Checklist
  1. Set unique Bundle Identifier and version number in Player Settings.
  2. Configure and backup keystore for Android; select proper signing keys.
  3. Test signed builds on real devices and in the target browser for WebGL.
  4. Prepare store assets and metadata separate from the build itself.
Common Mistake

Building release APK without configuring the keystore or using a debug key prevents publishing and can block updates.

screens.title: Testing Builds on Devices and Debugging Outside the Editor
screens.narratorSegment: Testing a build on the real target hardware is essential because the Unity editor hides runtime differences. For example, performance, input handling, file paths, and graphics behavior can change on a user's machine or a mobile device. Start by running the built executable or installing the signed APK on a device and exercise the core flows. To inspect runtime logs on Windows, check the Player log or redirect logs to a file via Player Settings if needed. For mobile devices, use Android logcat or Xcode device logs to read Debug. Log output and crash traces. For WebGL, open the browser developer console to read logs and catch JavaScript errors. Performance profiling is a different step: use the Unity Profiler connected to a running build or platform-specific profilers to find spikes and garbage collection pauses. A practical tip: reduce build size and speed up iterations by enabling development build and script debugging during early tests; these builds run slower but provide stack traces and readable logs. However, never ship release builds with development flags enabled. Common pitfalls include not testing the final signed package, assuming Editor performance equals device performance, and overlooking platform-specific input or permission prompts. Always test on a device with similar specs to your target audience and run a smoke test of all scenes and menus. After testing, capture a clear list of differences and reproduce them back in the editor with platform emulation or targeted debugging. What is one log message you would search for first when a building crashes on startup?

content.html:
Module 6 › Testing & Debugging

Testing Builds on Devices and Debugging Outside the Editor

How to gather logs, profile performance, and reproduce issues found only in builds.

Eyebrow: Testing & Debugging
Where to Read Logs
  • Windows/Mac: Player log in user data folders or use redirected logs from Player Settings.
  • Android: Use logcat to view Debug.Log and exception traces.
  • iOS: Read device logs through Xcode's device console.
  • WebGL: Open the browser developer console to see logs and errors.
Profiler & Performance Checks
  1. Run the Unity Profiler attached to a development build on device to capture frame timings.
  2. Look for long GC spikes and expensive rendering calls.
  3. Test on devices with target hardware profiles to capture realistic performance.
Quick Diagnostic Steps
Reproduce the crash and immediately capture the platform log for the timestamp.
Enable Development Build to get stack traces and enable the Profiler if needed.
Confirm all scenes are present in the build; a missing scene may show a blank screen but no error.
Try This

For WebGL, run a simple local server like python -m http.server and open the page to avoid file-protocol restrictions.

screens.title: Asset Bundles: Manual Packaging for Dynamic Content
screens.narratorSegment: Asset Bundles are Unity packages that archive assets so they can be loaded at runtime rather than being baked into the main build. Use Asset Bundles when you need to reduce initial download size or provide optional downloadable content like new levels, large textures, or seasonal assets. They are platform-specific, so you build bundles for each target platform. The workflow is manual: you mark assets for bundling, configure bundle names or variants, and then run a build process that produces package files you can host remotely. The advantage is fine-grained control and predictable file layout. The downsides are that you must manage dependencies, handle caching, and manually orchestrate bundle creation and versioning. If you forget to include a dependency or mismatch a platform build of the bundle, you may encounter missing-asset errors at runtime. Typical mistakes include storing bundles in the wrong place, not rebuilding bundles after asset changes, and serving mismatched platform bundles to clients. For projects with modest dynamic content, Asset Bundles work well, but the overhead of bundle management grows with project complexity. Asset Bundles are a powerful tool when you need strict control over packaging, but they require extra automation and careful versioning. Consider how often your content will change and whether the manual management effort is worth the control it provides.

content.html:
Module 6 › Asset Bundles

Asset Bundles: Manual Packaging for Dynamic Content

A low-level way to package assets for runtime loading that requires manual management.

Definition & Workflow
  1. Mark assets with an Asset Bundle name in the Inspector.
  2. Run the AssetBundle build pipeline for the target platform.
  3. Host the resulting bundle files on a server or include them with the game.
  4. Load bundles at runtime and instantiate assets from them.
When to Choose Asset Bundles
  • You need tight control over packaging and file layout.
  • You have few remote updates and can manage bundle lifecycle manually.
  • You want minimal abstraction and predictable asset filenames.
Common Pitfalls
  • Forgetting to rebuild bundles after changing assets.
  • Serving bundles for the wrong platform to clients.
  • Neglecting dependency management, causing runtime missing assets.
Analogy

Think of Asset Bundles like zip files you create by hand; they are flexible but you must maintain the zips and their versions yourself.

screens.title: Addressables: Modern Workflow and Loading Example
screens.narratorSegment: Addressables build on Asset Bundles to make packaging and runtime loading far easier. Instead of manually naming bundles and tracking dependencies, you mark assets as Addressable in the Inspector and give them a string address. Unity then manages bundle creation, dependency graphs, caching, and remote hosting abstractions. At runtime you request an asset by its address and the system fetches and caches the necessary bundles. This removes much of the manual bookkeeping. A concrete example is loading a player prefab called MyPlayerCharacter. In code you call Addressables. LoadAssetAsync ("MyPlayerCharacter"); then handle the completed operation to instantiate the result. Addressables also support remote catalogs and automatic updates, which suit live-service games or frequent content pushes. Common misconceptions are that Addressables remove the need to think about bundle size or platform builds; they help, but you still must produce bundles for each platform and design your remote hosting strategy. Also, early adopter projects sometimes misconfigure addresses or forget to check dependencies in the Addressables Groups window. The recommended approach is to mark high-level assets as addressable, test local and remote profiles, and allow Addressables to manage caching and dependencies. This yields faster iteration and safer live content updates compared to manual bundles.

content.html:
Module 6 › Addressables

Addressables: Modern Workflow and Loading Example

A code-focused view of how Addressables let you request assets by address and handle caching automatically.

Eyebrow: Addressables
Addressables Example
// Example: load a prefab marked as Addressable
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.AddressableAssets;
using UnityEngine.ResourceManagement.AsyncOperations;

public class LoadPlayer : MonoBehaviour
{
  void Start()
  {
    Addressables.LoadAssetAsync<GameObject>("MyPlayerCharacter").Completed += OnLoaded;
  }

  private void OnLoaded(AsyncOperationHandle<GameObject> handle)
  {
    if (handle.Status == AsyncOperationStatus.Succeeded)
    {
      Instantiate(handle.Result);
    }
    else
    {
      Debug.Log("Failed to load addressable asset.");
    }
  }
}
The Addressables system handles the bundle download and caches the result. You can configure remote profiles and update catalogs without changing code addresses.
Best Practices
  • Use clear, stable addresses for production assets.
  • Group assets by update cadence to minimize remotes downloads.
  • Test both local and remote profiles before releasing live updates.
Why Addressables?
  • Automates bundle dependency tracking and caching.
  • Enables remote hosting and catalog updates without code changes.
  • Simplifies runtime loading via string addresses.
Common Mistake

Marking everything as addressable can create many small bundles and overhead; group assets logically by update frequency instead.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap the most important ideas you should remember as you prepare to ship games. First, Build Settings are the control center for choosing target platforms and the scenes to include. Always verify your scene list and platform selection before building because missing scenes are a common cause of runtime gaps. Second, Player Settings control how your game identifies itself to the OS and stores critical metadata like the Bundle Identifier and keystore configuration; these values are essential for mobile store publishing. Third, build outputs differ by platform: executables plus data folders for desktop, APK or AAB for Android, Xcode projects and signed IPAs for iOS, and H T M L plus JavaScript and data files for WebGL — each requires platform-appropriate testing and hosting. Keep these three concepts in mind as a quick checklist when packaging and testing your builds.

content.html:
Module 6 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts

Three compact reminders to guide builds and distribution decisions.

Build Settings
Select target platform and included scenes; a correct scene list prevents missing content in builds.
Player Settings
Controls identity, version, icons, and platform-specific flags like Bundle Identifier and keystore settings.
Build Outputs
Desktop builds use executables and data folders; mobile and web have their own packaging and hosting needs.
Takeaway

Before you build for release: confirm scenes, set identity and signing, and run the build on the target platform to verify behavior.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: A few final reminders about content delivery and common mistakes. First, keystores are critical: keep them safe and back them up because losing the keystore prevents updating published Android apps. Second, Asset Bundles give you manual control and are platform-specific; they are useful when you want predictable packaging but require you to manage dependencies and versions. Third, Addressables simplify asset management by automating bundling, dependency tracking, caching, and remote catalog updates, making them the recommended approach for dynamic content in most modern projects. Remember too that whether you use bundles or Addressables you must still build asset packages for each target platform and test them like any other build. Keep your build logs handy, test on actual target devices, and avoid shipping debug builds to production. These steps prevent many common distribution failures and make post-release updates much smoother.

Module 6 › What to Remember

What to Remember

Three short reminders to keep your releases safe and maintainable.

Keystore Safety
Back up keystores and never lose the signing key used for published apps.
Asset Bundles
Good for manual control, but remember to rebuild per platform and manage dependencies.
Addressables
Use Addressables to simplify remote updates, caching, and dependency handling for dynamic content.
Closing Thought

Treat builds as deliverables: sign them correctly, host them appropriately, and always verify on the same platform your players will use.

fullNarratorScript:
Bringing a game to players means more than finishing levels and scripts. In this lesson you will learn the practical steps to turn your Unity project into an app or executable for Windows, WebGL, Android and other targets. We will use Unity's Build Settings and Player Settings as the control center: select target platforms, add scenes, and set identity and presentation options like company name, product name, icons, and splash screens. You'll also learn about platform requirements such as the Android SDK, NDK and JDK, and how different targets produce different output files — a Windows executable and data folder, a WebGL folder of H T M L and JavaScript, or a signed Android APK. Finally, we'll introduce runtime content strategies: Asset Bundles and Addressables, which let you deliver large or updated content without rebuilding the whole game. By the end you should understand how to configure builds, what can fail, and where to test. Think about a target platform you care about — what is the smallest change that would let you run your game there?

By the end of this section you will be able to prepare and execute platform builds, configure player identity and presentation, and plan distribution steps for desktop, web, and mobile. First, you'll learn to configure Unity's Build Settings to select target platforms and include the correct scenes. That matters because missing scenes or wrong targets are one of the most common build-time mistakes. Second, you'll learn how to customize Player Settings for company name, product name, icons and splash screens so your app presents correctly to users and stores. Third, you'll run the build process to create executables or app bundles and inspect the produced files. Finally, you'll begin to plan post-build steps like signing APKs, hosting WebGL files, and testing on devices. Each skill reduces friction when you deliver to players. For example, setting a correct Bundle Identifier prevents store upload errors; testing the build on hardware reveals performance differences the editor won't show. Keep these goals handy as we move into the practical steps.

This second objectives slide explains how you will prove competency. For configuring Build Settings, you'll show you can pick a platform and add scenes so the built game contains the intended content. A concrete example: add MainScene and build a Windows executable that runs the rotating cube scene. For Player Settings, you'll set Company Name and Product Name so the OS and task manager show the expected labels, and assign a default icon so your executable has a custom icon. For executing builds, you'll create Build folders for Windows and WebGL, run the builds, and verify the output files open or can be hosted locally. Finally, for content delivery, you'll describe where Addressables would fit — mark assets as Addressable and explain how remote hosting lets you update content without a full rebuild. Common misconceptions to avoid: treating Editor play as equivalent to a real build, or skipping keystore configuration for mobile. Each objective ends with a short practical milestone you can demonstrate or explain.

Unity's Build Settings window is the central hub that turns your project into a platform-specific package. A build includes scenes, compiled C# scripts, processed assets, and platform libraries. To create a build you first select a target platform — for example, Windows Standalone, WebGL, Android or iOS — then add the scenes you want included. Adding a scene to the Build Settings ensures its content is packaged in the final build. Different platforms cause Unity to re-import or re-compile assets with target-specific options, so switching platforms may take time. A concrete example: selecting WebGL and adding MainScene produces an H T M L/JavaScript/data folder suitable for hosting on a web server. A common misconception is to rely solely on editor play: editor behavior can mask platform differences such as file input and output or graphics support. Another important point: some platforms require external tooling; building Android needs a configured Android SDK, NDK and a JDK in Unity Preferences. If those are missing, builds will fail or warn. Takeaway: treat Build Settings as an explicit checklist — pick the platform, verify scenes, and confirm any required SDKs before pressing Build. How might you verify the correct scenes are included without running the full game?

Player Settings control how your game identifies itself to the operating system and to players. Core fields include Company Name and Product Name; these values affect the executable title, task manager entries, and store listing metadata. You also set Version, Default Icon and the Splash Image here. For standalone builds you control Resolution and Presentation — default screen size, fullscreen mode, and whether the player window is resizable. Platform-specific sections expose important options: Android shows Bundle Identifier, Minimum and Target A P I Levels, Scripting Backend choices like Mono or IL2CPP, architectures such as ARMv7 or ARM64, and Keystore configuration for signing APKs. WebGL has Compression Format, Memory Size and Template options. A concrete example: in the hands-on we set Company Name to "Cohortia" and Product Name to "MyAwesomeGame" so the produced executable shows that identity. A common mistake is forgetting the Bundle Identifier or keystore for mobile uploads; this blocks publishing. Takeaway: set identity values early and keep platform-specific settings in your release checklist so builds and store submissions are consistent. Player Settings — identity and presentation means player settings determine user-facing identity and many platform-specific build requirements; set them deliberately to avoid store and runtime issues.. In practical terms, company name, product name, icons, splash, and per-platform options. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Different platforms require different tooling, outputs and testing strategies. Android builds require platform toolchains: the Android SDK, NDK and a Java Development Kit must be installed and configured in Unity's Preferences. You also need to set a Bundle Identifier (a unique string such as com. YourCompany. YourGame), pick minimum and target A P I levels, choose a scripting backend (Mono for faster iteration, IL2CPP for performance and compatibility), select supported architectures and configure a Keystore to sign your APK. Closing question: what platform-specific checklist will you run before your next build?

Sometimes you need platform-specific behavior in C#. Unity's preprocessor directives let you include or exclude code at compile time depending on the selected build target. Common misconceptions are that Addressables remove the need to think about bundle size or platform builds; they help, but you still must produce bundles for each platform and design your remote hosting strategy. Also, early adopter projects sometimes misconfigure addresses or forget to check dependencies in the Addressables Groups window. The recommended approach is to mark high-level assets as addressable, test local and remote profiles, and allow Addressables to manage caching and dependencies. This yields faster iteration and safer live content updates compared to manual bundles.

Let's recap the most important ideas you should remember as you prepare to ship games. First, Build Settings are the control center for choosing target platforms and the scenes to include. Always verify your scene list and platform selection before building because missing scenes are a common cause of runtime gaps. Second, Player Settings control how your game identifies itself to the OS and stores critical metadata like the Bundle Identifier and keystore configuration; these values are essential for mobile store publishing. Third, build outputs differ by platform: executables plus data folders for desktop, APK or AAB for Android, Xcode projects and signed IPAs for iOS, and H T M L plus JavaScript and data files for WebGL — each requires platform-appropriate testing and hosting. Keep these three concepts in mind as a quick checklist when packaging and testing your builds.

A few final reminders about content delivery and common mistakes. First, keystores are critical: keep them safe and back them up because losing the keystore prevents updating published Android apps. Second, Asset Bundles give you manual control and are platform-specific; they are useful when you want predictable packaging but require you to manage dependencies and versions. Third, Addressables simplify asset management by automating bundling, dependency tracking, caching, and remote catalog updates, making them the recommended approach for dynamic content in most modern projects. Remember too that whether you use bundles or Addressables you must still build asset packages for each target platform and test them like any other build. Keep your build logs handy, test on actual target devices, and avoid shipping debug builds to production. These steps prevent many common distribution failures and make post-release updates much smoother.
